paragraphs: So get this, this all went down back in the day with this king named Xerxes. This dude was the ruler of a massive empire that stretched all the way from India to Ethiopia—like, 127 different regions. King Xerxes was chilling on his throne in the capital city, Susa.
In his third year as king, he decided to throw a huge banquet for all his officials and ministers. The top military guys from Persia and Media were there, plus all the princes and governors.

For a solid six months, he was just showing off, putting on display all the crazy rich stuff his kingdom had and how stunningly beautiful his royal palace was. After that massive display, the king threw another party, this one for a whole week, for every single person living in the capital, Susa—didn't matter if you were a big shot or a nobody. The party was in the super fancy garden courtyard of the king's summer house. The whole place was decked out with white and blue cotton curtains, tied up with linen and purple cords to silver rings on marble pillars. They had couches made of silver and gold set up on this insane mosaic floor made of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and colored stones. Drinks were served in solid gold cups, and get this—every single cup was one of a kind. The royal wine was flowing like water, 'cause the king was being super generous.

Basically, you could drink as much as you wanted. The king ordered the waiters to just keep refilling everyone's cup. Meanwhile, Queen Vashti was having her own party for the women inside King Xerxes's royal palace.

On the seventh and final day of the party, the king, who was pretty drunk by this point, told his seven personal eunuch servants—Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas—to go get Queen Vashti. He wanted her to come out wearing her royal crown so he could show off to all his guests how beautiful she was. And yeah, she was absolutely stunning.

But Queen Vashti was like, 'Nah,' and straight up refused to come. She rejected the king's order that the servants delivered. The king completely lost it. He was absolutely fuming that she would disrespect him like that. So, he called in his advisors, who were all experts on the law. It was his thing to always ask his experts for advice. His inner circle included guys named Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan—the seven most powerful princes of Persia and Media who could always talk to the king. He asked them what legal options they had against Queen Vashti for ignoring King Xerxes's summons delivered by the eunuchs.

Then this guy Memucan spoke up in front of the king and all the other princes: “Look, Queen Vashti didn't just disrespect you, King. She dissed all of us, all the leaders and all the people in every single one of your provinces. The news is gonna spread like wildfire: ‘Yo, did you hear about Queen Vashti? King Xerxes told her to come, and she just said no!’ When other women hear this, they're all gonna start treating their own husbands with zero respect. The day the wives of the Persian and Mede officials hear what the queen did, they'll be out of control. Is that what we really want? A whole country full of angry women who don't know their place?”

“So, if you're cool with it, King, you should make a royal decree. Have it recorded in the laws of the Persians and Medes so it can never be revoked. The law should say that Vashti is permanently banned from King Xerxes' presence. And then, you should give her royal title to a woman who knows her place. When this new rule is announced all over your massive kingdom, every single woman, no matter if she's rich or poor, will have to show proper respect to her husband.”

The king and his princes were all like, 'Yeah, that's a great idea.' So the king did exactly what Memucan suggested. He sent out messages to every part of his kingdom, written in each province's own script and in their own language. The message was clear: “Every man is the boss in his own house, and whatever he says, goes. Period.”

title: The Royal Rise: From Zero to Hero

paragraphs: So, after a while, King Xerxes wasn't as mad at Queen Vashti anymore. He was having second thoughts about what Vashti had done and what he'd ordered against her. His crew of young assistants saw their chance and were like, “Yo, let's find some amazing, beautiful young women for the king.” They suggested the king get officials in every part of his kingdom to bring all the beautiful, single ladies to the palace in Susa. They'd go to the harem, which was run by this guy Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the women. He'd get them all set up with spa treatments and everything. Then, the girl who pleases the king the most would become the new queen instead of Vashti.
The king was totally on board with this plan and made it happen.

Now, there was this Jewish guy named Mordecai living in the palace complex in Susa. He was Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish—a Benjaminite. His ancestors had been taken from Jerusalem into exile along with King Jehoiachin of Judah when King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon carried them off. Mordecai had raised his cousin, Hadassah, who everyone called Esther, because she had no father or mother. She had a great figure and a beautiful face. After her parents died, Mordecai adopted her.
When the king's new rule went public, a ton of young women were brought to the palace in Susa and handed over to Hegai. Esther was one of them.

Hegai thought Esther was awesome and took a real liking to her. He immediately started her on the best beauty treatments, got her special food, gave her seven personal maids from the palace, and put her and her maids in the best suite in the harem. But Esther kept her family and her Jewish background on the down-low, because Mordecai told her not to say anything.
Every single day, Mordecai would walk by the harem courtyard to check in and see how Esther was doing and what was going on with her.

Each girl had to complete twelve months of beauty prep before her turn to meet King Xerxes. It was six months of treatments with myrrh oil, and then six months with perfumes and other cosmetics. When a girl's time came to go to the king, she could take whatever she wanted with her from the harem to the king's quarters. She'd go to his place in the evening and then in the morning, she'd move to a second harem, this one run by Shaashgaz, another one of the king's eunuchs who was in charge of the concubines. A girl would never see the king again unless he was super into her and specifically asked for her by name.

When it was Esther's turn to go to the king—Esther, the daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle, who had adopted her as his daughter—she asked for nothing other than what Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the harem, recommended. And just like that, Esther, just as she was, wowed everyone who saw her.
She was taken to King Xerxes in his royal palace in the tenth month, the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of the king's reign.

The king was head over heels for Esther, way more than any of the other women. He was completely smitten. He put a royal crown on her head and made her the new queen, replacing Vashti. Then the king threw a huge party for all his nobles and officials, calling it “Esther’s Banquet.” He even declared a public holiday for the whole kingdom and gave out tons of generous gifts.

On one of the occasions when the virgins were being gathered, Mordecai was just chilling at the King's Gate. The whole time, Esther had kept her family background and her race a secret, just like Mordecai told her to. She still listened to him, just like when she was a kid.

So on this particular day, while Mordecai was at the King's Gate, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the entrance, Bigthana and Teresh, were plotting to kill King Xerxes. But Mordecai found out about their plan and told Queen Esther. She then went and told the king, making sure to give Mordecai the credit. The whole thing was investigated, and it turned out to be true, so the two guys were hanged. And this was all written down in the king's official records.

title: The King's Advisor Goes on a Power Trip
changes: EN p0: second most powerful→highest-ranking official (MSG 원문)
EN p5: Haman son of Hammedatha 복원, 배지 11→10
paragraphs: A little while later, King Xerxes gave a major promotion to this guy Haman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite. He basically made him the highest-ranking official in the whole government. All the king's staff at the main gate would bow down and kneel whenever Haman came by—that was the king's direct order.

But Mordecai? Nah, he wasn't having it. He refused to bow down. The other royal staff were like, "Dude, why are you disobeying the king's command?" They bugged him about it every single day, but he just wouldn't listen. So, they told Haman, thinking something had to be done. Mordecai had already told them he was a Jew.

When Haman saw with his own eyes that Mordecai wasn't bowing down, he was seriously ticked off. But then he found out Mordecai was a Jew, and suddenly, getting mad at just one guy felt like a waste of energy. He decided to go bigger—he started plotting how to get rid of not just Mordecai, but every single Jew in Xerxes' entire kingdom.

So, in the first month, Nisan, during Xerxes' twelfth year as king, Haman had them cast a "pur"—which is like drawing lots—to pick the perfect day and month for his evil plan. The lot fell on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is Adar.

Haman then went to King Xerxes and said, "Hey King, there's this weird group of people scattered all over your kingdom, and they just don't fit in. Their traditions are totally different from everyone else's. And what's worse, they totally ignore your laws. It's a disgrace, and you shouldn't let them get away with it. If you're cool with it, let's just issue an order to wipe them out. I'll even pay for the whole thing myself. I'll drop 375 tons of silver into the royal treasury to cover the costs."
The king just took off his special signet ring and handed it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the number one enemy of the Jews.
"Go for it," the king told Haman. "It's your money. Do whatever you want with those people."

So on the thirteenth day of the first month, the king's secretaries were called in. They wrote down every single word of Haman's order, addressing it to all the king's satraps, governors, and officials of every single province and people group. It was written in their own languages and scripts, in King Xerxes' name, and sealed with his royal ring.

Bulletins were sent out by couriers to every province in the kingdom. The orders were to massacre, kill, and completely wipe out all the Jews—young, old, women, and children—on one single day: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar. And, they were allowed to take all their stuff. Copies of the bulletin were posted in public in every province, so everyone could get ready for that day.
At the king's command, the couriers took off; the order was also posted in the palace complex of Susa. The king and Haman sat back and had a drink while the city of Susa reeled from the news.

title: If I Die, I Die
changes: EN p2: a single rule·The one exception·thirty days 복원, 배지 10-12→9-11
EN p3: will be toast→will be wiped out, 배지 13-15→12-14

paragraphs: When Mordecai found out what was going down, he totally lost it. He ripped his clothes, threw on some rough old burlap, and covered himself in ashes. Then he went through the city, wailing super loud and bitter. He could only go as far as the King’s Gate, though, because you weren’t allowed in wearing that kind of outfit. And as the king’s new rule got posted everywhere, all the Jewish people were in major mourning—they were fasting, crying, and just falling apart. Most of them were just lying on the ground in burlap and ashes.

Esther’s maids and personal assistants came and told her what was up. The queen was shocked. She sent Mordecai some fresh clothes so he could change out of the burlap, but he was like, “Nah.” So Esther called for this guy Hathach, one of the king's assistants assigned to her, and told him to go find out from Mordecai what was really going on. Hathach went to Mordecai in the town square right by the King’s Gate. Mordecai spilled everything that had happened to him. He even told him the exact amount of cash Haman had promised to pay the king to get all the Jews killed. Mordecai also gave him a copy of the official order for the massacre that was posted in Susa, so he could show it to Esther and tell her she had to go to the king and beg him to save her people.

Hathach went back and told Esther everything Mordecai said. Esther talked it over with Hathach and then sent him back to Mordecai with this message: “Look, everyone who works for the king, and even people out in the provinces, knows the deal. There's a single rule for any man or woman who just shows up to the king without an invite: they die. The one exception is if the king holds out his gold scepter to them; then they get to live. And it's been thirty days now since I've been invited to come to the king.”

When Hathach told Mordecai what Esther said, Mordecai sent this message back to her: “Don’t think for a second that just because you’re in the palace, you’re the one Jew who’s gonna make it out of this alive. If you stay quiet at a time like this, help will come for the Jews from somewhere else, but you and your family will be wiped out. Who knows? Maybe you were made queen for this exact moment.”

Esther sent her answer back to Mordecai: “Go get all the Jews in Susa together. Fast for me. Don’t eat or drink anything for three days and three nights. Me and my maids will do the same. After that, I’ll go to the king, even though it’s against the law. If I die, I die.”
Mordecai bounced and did everything Esther told him to do.

title: Esther's Risky Dinner Party

paragraphs: Three days later, Esther got all dressed up in her royal robes and went to the inner court of the palace, right in front of the king's throne room. The king was on his throne, facing the entrance. When he saw Queen Esther standing there, he was actually glad to see her and held out the golden scepter in his hand. Esther went up and touched the tip of it.
The king asked, "And what's your desire, Queen Esther? What do you want? Just ask, and you'll get it—even if it's half of my kingdom!"
Esther said, "If it's cool with you, I'd like for you and Haman to come to a dinner I've made for you."
"Get Haman right away," the king said, "so we can go to dinner with Esther."
So the king and Haman went to the dinner Esther had set up. While they were drinking wine, the king said, "Okay, for real, what do you want? You can have up to half my kingdom. Just ask!"
Esther replied, "So, here's what I want. If you're really down to do this for me, please come with Haman to the dinner I'll make for you tomorrow. Then I'll tell you what I really want."

Haman left the palace that day feeling super happy. But then he saw Mordecai at the King's Gate, who completely ignored him. Haman was seriously mad at Mordecai, but he kept his cool and went home. He gathered his friends and his wife Zeresh and started bragging about how rich he was, his many sons, all the honors the king had given him, and how he was promoted to the top job in the government. "And get this," Haman went on, "Queen Esther invited me to a private dinner with the king, just the three of us. And she invited me again tomorrow. But none of that matters when I see that guy Mordecai the Jew sitting at the King's Gate."

His wife Zeresh and all his friends were like, "You should build a gallows that's 75 feet high. First thing in the morning, talk to the king and get him to hang Mordecai on it. Then you can go to dinner with the king and actually enjoy it."
Haman thought that was a great idea. So he had the gallows built.

paragraphs: So that night, the king was tossing and turning and just could not sleep. He told his servants to bring the official records, like the kingdom's daily journal, and read it to him. They got to the part where Mordecai totally saved the day by exposing the plot of Bigthana and Teresh—the two eunuchs who guarded the entrance and had conspired to assassinate King Xerxes.
The king stops them and asks, "Wait, what did we do for Mordecai for this? What kind of big reward did he get?"
His servants were like, "Uh, nothing. Literally nothing was done for him."
The king says, "Is anyone in the courtyard right now?"
And guess who just walked in? Haman. He was coming to the outer court to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he'd just built for him. Talk about awkward timing.
The servants go, "Yeah, Haman's out there waiting."
"Send him in," the king says.
When Haman comes in, the king asks him, "Hey, what should I do for someone I really, really want to honor?"

Haman's thinking to himself, "He's talking about me! Who else could it be?" So he goes all out and says, "For the guy the king wants to honor, you should totally do this: Get a royal robe the king himself has worn, and a horse the king has ridden, one with a royal crown on its head. Then, have one of the king's most noble princes put the robe on the guy, lead him on the horse through the main city square, and shout, 'This is what happens when the king wants to honor someone!'"

"Great idea!" the king says to Haman. "Go do that. Right now. Take the robe and the horse and do everything you just said for Mordecai the Jew, the one who hangs out at the King's Gate. And don't you dare skip a single detail."

So Haman had to take the robe and horse, dress up Mordecai, and lead him through the city square, yelling, "This is what is done for the man whom the king especially wants to honor!" The ultimate humiliation.

After the parade, Mordecai just went back to his post at the King's Gate like it was no big deal. But Haman? He sprinted home, completely mortified, hiding his face in shame. He told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened, and his knowledgeable friends and his wife Zeresh were like, "Dude, if this Mordecai guy is in fact a Jew, you're finished. Your bad luck is just getting started. You have zero chance against him—you're basically ruined."
And while they were still talking, the king's guys showed up to rush Haman to the dinner Esther had prepared. It was all happening so fast.

paragraphs: So, the king and Haman rolled up to Queen Esther's dinner party. During the second dinner, while they were sipping on some wine, the king asked again, “Queen Esther, for real, what do you want? I'll give you half of my kingdom! Just say the word, and it's yours.”
Queen Esther answered, “If you're really cool with me, O King, and if you're down, please spare my life, and spare my people's lives.

“We've been sold out, me and my people, to be totally destroyed—like, massacred and eliminated. If we were just being sold as slaves, I wouldn't have even brought it up; our problems wouldn't have been a big enough deal to bother you with.”
King Xerxes totally lost it and was like, “Who? Where is this guy? This is messed up!”
“An enemy. An adversary. This evil Haman,” said Esther.
Haman was shocked, standing there in front of the king and queen.
The king was so mad he left his wine and stormed out into the palace garden.

Haman stayed behind, begging Queen Esther for his life—he knew the king was done with him and that he was finished. Just as the king was coming back from the garden into the banquet hall, Haman was basically throwing himself on the couch where Esther was chilling. The king yelled, “Are you seriously going to assault the queen while I'm right here?!”
The second the king said that, Haman went pale.

Harbona, one of the guys who worked for the king, spoke up: “Look at this! There’s that huge gallows that Haman built for Mordecai, the guy who saved the king’s life. It’s right next to Haman’s house—like, 75 feet tall!”
The king said, “Hang him on it!”
So they hanged Haman on the very gallows he had built for Mordecai. And the king finally chilled out.

title: The Tables Have Turned: Payback Time!
changes: EN p1: Haman the Agagite·bulletins authorizing the plan of Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite 복원 (MSG 8:3, 8:5)
EN p5: in all King Xerxes' provinces 복원 (MSG 8:13)

paragraphs: On the very same day, King Xerxes handed over all of Haman's property to Queen Esther—you know, Haman, the archenemy of the Jewish people. And then Mordecai got to come before the king, because Esther finally told him that they were family. The king took off his special signet ring, the one he'd taken back from Haman, and gave it straight to Mordecai. To top it off, Esther put Mordecai in charge of Haman's entire estate. Talk about a major glow-up.

But Esther wasn't finished. She went back to the king, fell at his feet, and was literally in tears, begging him to undo the evil plan Haman the Agagite had cooked up to destroy the Jews. The king held out his golden scepter to her, so she stood up and said, “Look, if you’re cool with it, and if you actually care about me and think this is the right thing to do, please, can you send out an official order to cancel the bulletins authorizing the plan of Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite to annihilate the Jews in all the king's provinces? I seriously can't handle watching my people get wiped out. How can I just stand by and see my own relatives get massacred?”

King Xerxes told Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew, “Look, I’ve already given Haman’s estate to Esther, and he’s been executed because he tried to mess with the Jews. So now, you guys can write a new order for the Jews, whatever you think is best. Then seal it with my ring.” (Anything written in the king’s name and sealed with his ring was legit and couldn't be taken back.)

So on the 23rd day of the third month, Sivan, the king’s secretaries were called in. A new order was written exactly as Mordecai dictated. It was sent out to all the satraps, governors, and officials of the 127 provinces from India all the way to Ethiopia. They wrote it in each province's own script and language, and of course, for the Jews in their own script and language too.
He wrote it all under King Xerxes' name and sealed it with the royal signet ring. Then he sent out the bulletins by messengers on super-fast horses, the best of the best from the king's own stables.

The king's new order gave the Jews in every city the green light to arm themselves and fight back. They could defend themselves to the death, kill anyone who threatened them, their women, or their children, and they could even take all the stuff their enemies owned. The day set for this in all King Xerxes' provinces was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar. The order was posted publicly in every province so everyone knew what was up, and the Jews could get ready to get their revenge on their enemies.
The messengers, hyped up by the king's command, took off on their royal horses like it was a race. At the same time, the new rule was posted all over the palace in Susa.

Mordecai walked out of the king's presence looking magnificent in a royal robe of violet and white, a massive gold crown, and a purple cape of fine linen. The whole city of Susa just erupted with joy. For the Jews, it was a time for celebration, laughter, and being honored. It was like that everywhere, in every province and city where the king's order was announced. The Jews were partying in the streets, cheering and feasting. And get this—a lot of non-Jews even converted and became Jews, because suddenly it was pretty dangerous *not* to be one.

title: The Ultimate Payback: Purim Origin Story

splits.note: MSG 9:1-4 한 문단을 날짜·역전 선언(1-4) / 성읍 집결·관리 지원(1-4)으로 분할. 내용 손실 없음.

KO p8: 음식을 나눠 먹고→선물을 주고받고, 아하수에로→크세르크세스
paragraphs: On the thirteenth day of Adar (the twelfth month), the day the king's order was supposed to go live, everything got flipped. This was the day the Jews' enemies were planning to totally own them, but the tables turned, big time. The Jews ended up owning the people who hated them.

The Jews gathered in their cities all over King Xerxes' kingdom to take down anyone who was trying to ruin them. Literally no one could stand up to them—fear made cowards of them all. On top of that, all the government officials, the satraps, the governors—basically everyone working for the king—were quietly helping the Jews because they were scared of Mordecai. By this point, Mordecai was a major player in the palace, and his reputation was growing everywhere.

So, the Jews absolutely wrecked their enemies with swords, just a complete slaughter, and did whatever they wanted to the people who hated them. In the capital city of Susa, the Jews took out five hundred men. They also killed the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the archenemy of the Jews: Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha.

But here's the thing: they didn't take any of their stuff. That day, after it was all over, the king got the final body count from the capital. The king said to Queen Esther, "Just in Susa alone, the Jews have killed five hundred men, plus Haman's ten sons. It's wild to think about the numbers in the rest of the kingdom! So, what else do you want? Just say the word, and it's yours. Your wish is my command."

Queen Esther replied, "If it's cool with you, King, could you give the Jews in Susa permission to keep this going for one more day? Oh, and also, hang the bodies of Haman's ten sons on the gallows for everyone to see."
The king commanded it. The order was extended, and the bodies of Haman's ten sons were hung up in public.
The Jews in Susa went back at it. On the 14th of Adar, they killed another three hundred men in Susa. But again, they didn't take any loot.

Meanwhile, in the rest of the king's provinces, the Jews had teamed up to defend themselves and break free from their oppressors. On the 13th of Adar, they killed seventy-five thousand of their haters but, again, didn't take any of their stuff. The next day, the 14th, they chilled and had a huge party with tons of food and laughs. But in Susa, since the Jews had been fighting on both the 13th and 14th, they made the 15th their day to party. (This is why Jews who live out in the country celebrate on the 14th of Adar, making it a day for parties and giving gifts.)

Mordecai wrote all this down and sent letters to all the Jews in King Xerxes' provinces, no matter how far away. He told them to celebrate the 14th and 15th of Adar every year. This was to remember when the Jews got a break from their enemies, the month their sadness turned into joy, and their mourning turned into a holiday for parties, fun, laughter, and exchanging presents and giving gifts to the poor.
And they actually did it. What started then became a tradition, just like Mordecai had written to them.

Haman, son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the ultimate enemy of all Jews, had schemed to wipe them all out. He had cast the 'pur' (which means 'lot') to freak them out and destroy them. But when Queen Esther stepped in and talked to the king, he issued a written order that Haman's evil plan should totally backfire on him. He and his sons were hanged on the gallows. That's why these days are called 'Purim,' from the word 'pur' or 'lot.'

So, because of everything written in this letter and everything they had gone through, the Jews agreed to keep it going. It became a tradition for them, their kids, and anyone who joined them later to remember these two days every year on the exact dates written in the letter. These days are meant to be remembered and celebrated by every generation, every family, every province, and every city. These days of Purim must never be forgotten by the Jews; the memory of them must never fade away.

Then Queen Esther—Abihail's daughter—and Mordecai the Jew put their full authority behind a second letter about Purim to make it official. They sent letters to all the Jews in all 127 provinces of Xerxes' kingdom, with words of peace and truth, locking in these days of Purim on the exact dates set by Mordecai the Jew—dates they had agreed to for themselves and their descendants regarding their fasting and mourning. Esther's decree sealed the deal, and the whole thing was written down in the records.

paragraphs: King Xerxes was basically taxing his entire empire, from one end to the other. And all the other stuff about his reign, like all his big achievements and the full story of Mordecai's rise after the king promoted him—it's all written down in *The Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia.*

So yeah, Mordecai the Jew was basically the king's right-hand man, second only to King Xerxes himself. He was super popular with the Jewish people and they all looked up to him. He always worked hard for his people's best interests and made sure they were safe and thriving.
